clue.text: It's back to sleep without a programme to laugh at

indicators.note: back tells us the contraction for it is should be read from right to left

parts.note: it's can be written 'tis, the old contraction

indicators.note: without signals that the following letter is dropped from the sleep word

parts.note: a coma is a deep sleep

explanation.surface: Someone goes back to sleep rather than watch a comedy show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' is read as the old contraction 'tis; 'back' reverses it, and 'without a' drops the A from the sleep word.
explanation.definitionFit: A situation comedy is a television series made to amuse viewers.

clue.text: Queen seen as liable for damage

indicators.note: damage here means the letters of the phrase are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A queen is considered answerable for some damage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for damage' rearranges the eight letters of AS LIABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella of Castile was a famous Spanish monarch, sponsor of Columbus.

clue.text: False coin in old pouch

parts.note: cod as an adjective means sham or mock
a piece is a coin, as in a fifty-pence piece

explanation.surface: A counterfeit coin is found in an old purse.
explanation.walkthrough: COD as 'false' is British slang (a cod accent). A codpiece was a pouch on the front of men's breeches in Tudor times.
explanation.definitionFit: Tudor men wore a flap or bag at the front of their breeches, now a historical garment.

clue.text: Act, and risk being struck dumb

parts.note: to mum is to act in a mummers' play, a folk drama
a chance is a risk or gamble

explanation.surface: An actor takes a gamble and is left speechless.
explanation.walkthrough: Mumming is old English folk drama performed in disguise; to mum is to act in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Mumchance is an old word for silent or tongue-tied.

clue.text: For Lear, it was all advanced age

explanation.surface: King Lear's view of what matters in old age.
explanation.walkthrough: In King Lear, Edgar says 'Ripeness is all'; the quotation is attached to the play as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's line names maturity as everything; full maturity also describes being far along in years.

clue.text: They used to get stiff digging

definitions.text: They used to get stiff digging

parts.words: They used to get stiff digging
parts.note: stiff is slang for a corpse; these people dug up fresh bodies to sell to anatomists, a trade of the past

explanation.surface: Workers once grew stiff from hard digging.
explanation.walkthrough: Stiff looks like aching muscles, but it is a corpse: body-snatchers of the early 1800s dug up graves.
explanation.definitionFit: Body-snatchers who exhumed corpses for dissection were known by this name.

clue.text: Learned it in English — simple

indicators.note: in tells us the word it is placed inside the simple word

parts.note: rude can mean simple or primitive, as in a rude hut

explanation.surface: A learned word in English can still be plain.
explanation.walkthrough: Rude in the old sense of plain or unsophisticated, as in 'rude hut'; 'in' places the pronoun inside that word, after the E for English.
explanation.definitionFit: A scholarly, well-read person is described as having great erudition.

clue.text: Ten! Groggy man defeated rises from the floor

indicators.note: groggy means unsteady, so the three letters of ten are jumbled
in a down clue, rises means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a loser is a man who has been beaten

explanation.surface: A boxer counted out at ten struggles up off the canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groggy' makes ENT from TEN; 'rises' turns LOSER into RESOL. An entresol is a mezzanine floor.
explanation.definitionFit: An entresol is a mezzanine storey between the ground and first levels.

clue.text: A grass so wild it is a weed

indicators.note: wild means the letters of the phrase are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: A grass growing so freely counts as a weed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges A GRASS SO. Sargasso is a floating seaweed.
explanation.definitionFit: Sargasso is a brown seaweed that floats in large masses in the Atlantic.

clue.text: Court order: Amanda must avoid extremes

indicators.note: avoid extremes means the run sits inside the phrase, leaving off its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A court ruling requires Amanda to steer clear of extremes.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the first and last letters of AMANDA MUST leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandamus is a writ from a higher court commanding a lower body to perform a duty.

clue.text: He can kick better

explanation.surface: Someone who kicks the ball is an improvement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better' reads as 'superior', but it is someone who bets.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby or American football the kicker who drops and boots the ball has this name; it is also British slang for a gambler or customer.

clue.text: One who's dying to be a nuisance

explanation.surface: Someone desperate to be annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dying to' looks like 'eager to', but one sense is literally someone about to expire. In British slang the word means an annoying child.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally someone passing away; British slang for a pest or annoying little brat.

clue.text: Came in to adjust the screen

indicators.note: adjust means to rearrange, so the letters of the phrase are reordered

explanation.surface: Someone came in to fix the screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to adjust' rearranges CAME IN.
explanation.definitionFit: The screen is a collective name for films and the film industry, as is the picture house.

clue.text: Materialise out of thin air?

parts.note: taken literally, water vapour turns to liquid droplets out of the air

explanation.surface: Making something appear by magic.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means appear magically; read literally it is vapour becoming liquid.
explanation.definitionFit: Vapour turning to liquid is a physical change, so droplets do appear out of air.

clue.text: Fell over a stone, one being near

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the first piece above the second

parts.note: a fell is an animal's hide or skin
flint is a hard stone

explanation.surface: Someone tripped over a stone while standing close by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'near' means mean with money, not close by; 'Fell' is the noun for an animal's hide, not a tumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Near is an old word for stingy, and a miser is a stingy person.

clue.text: Proverbially, houses are so protected

parts.note: refers to the saying 'as ... as houses', meaning completely secure

explanation.surface: A remark on how secure homes are said to be.
explanation.walkthrough: The British phrase 'as safe as houses' means completely secure.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb compares something secure and protected to houses.

clue.text: Exhaust feature of gag

explanation.surface: Part of an exhaust system for a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gag' looks like a joke but means something that stops speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A muffler on a car exhaust deadens noise; a gag likewise stops someone making noise.

clue.text: Policeman lying over kick

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the first piece above the second

parts.note: flat means lying horizontal
to foot a ball is to kick it

explanation.surface: A policeman lying down is kicked.
explanation.walkthrough: Flatfoot is old slang for a policeman on the beat.
explanation.definitionFit: An old American slang term for a beat cop, from walking the streets.

clue.text: A band item from the past

parts.note: LSO is the London Symphony Orchestra, a band of musicians

explanation.surface: A piece from a band's old repertoire.
explanation.walkthrough: Item is an archaic word meaning likewise, used to introduce each entry in a list. LSO is the London Symphony Orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: Item once meant likewise or in addition, as in old inventories.

clue.text: In pain, as Gideon might be

indicators.note: might be suggests the letters of the phrase could form another word

explanation.surface: Gideon may be suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' rearranges AS GIDEON.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone suffering severe distress or anguish is described this way.

clue.text: Project meeting of deadly finality

explanation.surface: A project meeting where the outcome is final.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Project' looks like a scheme, but it is a verb: to stick out or shoot out.
explanation.definitionFit: To shoot out is to jut forward; a gunfight ending in death is likewise a decisive confrontation.

clue.text: Concentrating on cheap American jewellery?

parts.note: a cent is a small, cheap American coin
a ring is a piece of jewellery

explanation.surface: Focusing on inexpensive American trinkets.
explanation.walkthrough: A cent ring would be cheap American jewellery.
explanation.definitionFit: Bringing things to a central point means focusing them.

clue.text: Class a deadly sin as a big error

parts.note: cl. is a dictionary abbreviation for class
anger, or wrath, is one of the seven deadly sins

explanation.surface: Treating a deadly sin as a major blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: Clanger is British slang for a blunder, as in 'drop a clanger'.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a conspicuous blunder or gaffe.

clue.text: Team-member turns and runs off for catch

indicators.note: off means the letter for runs is removed
turns means the team-member word is reversed

parts.note: a partner is a member of a team
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A player wheels round and races off to take a catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' makes RENTRAP from PARTNER; 'off' drops R (runs) from it.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch someone in a trap or snare them.

clue.text: Occasionally see both sides

explanation.surface: Sometimes seeing both points of view.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the two halves of the field are the off side and the on side.
explanation.definitionFit: Intermittently means now and then; the two cricket field halves are named off and on.

clue.text: Coleridge, originally a lake poet

indicators.note: originally means the first letter of the poet's name is used

parts.note: lough is the Irish word for a lake

explanation.surface: Coleridge was at first a Lake poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lake poet' suggests Wordsworth's circle; the answer is Arthur Hugh Clough, a Victorian poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Hugh Clough was a Victorian poet.

clue.text: Circular armour against projectile

parts.note: mail is chain armour
shot is a projectile fired from a gun

explanation.surface: Round armour as a shield against missiles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circular' looks like an adjective (round armour) but is the noun for an advertising letter sent to many people.
explanation.definitionFit: A circular is a leaflet posted to many addresses at once.

clue.text: Charitable man? Rubbish — a heretic

parts.note: rot means nonsense or rubbish
an Arian is a follower of Arius, an early Christian heretic

explanation.surface: A man known for charity dismissed as a heretic.
explanation.walkthrough: Rotary clubs are known for charity work, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Rotary clubs raise funds for good causes.

clue.text: Meeting the latest requirements? Not up till now

indicators.note: not means the following word is removed from the phrase

parts.note: something fully modern is described as up to date
taken as written

explanation.surface: Not yet modern enough so far.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sentence gives UP TO DATE; 'Not up' removes UP.
explanation.definitionFit: So far, as at the present moment.
